fatal_errors: The proposed deformation intervention and 600 °C aging treatment are absent from the relevant 1100–1300 °C anneal-and-water-quench comparison.

The mechanism attributes phase formation to defect-assisted heterogeneous nucleation, whereas the observed reciprocal BCC/B2 structure is explained by composition-driven spinodal decomposition followed by Ni–Al ordering.
The proposed chronology is internally problematic: 10–20% cold work cannot straightforwardly be applied to an alloy still in its high-temperature BCC state 'prior to cooling.'
No prior evidence is supplied for the assumed low-dislocation, chemically uniform baseline or for dislocation density controlling phase stability in this alloy.
The hypothesis does not predict the observed increase in BCC fraction, ordered B2 precipitation, reciprocal Ni–Al versus Co–Cr–Fe partitioning, or monotonic hardness increase with quench temperature.
explanation: The answer presents a reasonably controlled undeformed-versus-deformed experiment with measurable variables and an explicit falsification rule, but it investigates a new deformation-assisted nucleation scenario rather than reconstructing the temperature-dependent transformation mechanism. It misses the central evidence: high-temperature BCC separation into Ni–Al-lean and Ni–Al-rich BCC products within a miscibility gap, possible sequential spinodal decomposition, subsequent B2 ordering, reciprocal nanoscale BCC/B2 distributions, and associated hardening. Its baseline is internally usable but is not the experimentally relevant 1100 °C annealed-and-quenched baseline or the undecomposed high-temperature BCC structural baseline. Because the alternative mechanism has no cited or alloy-specific support and rests on an ambiguous processing sequence, it is unsupported rather than a well-supported plausible alternative.
